    AI Overview
    Annual flu shots are recommended for everyone 6 months and older, ideally in September or October to allow two weeks for immunity to build. These vaccines prevent influenza infection, reduce symptom severity, and protect against circulating strains. Various options exist, including high-dose shots for seniors (65+) and a nasal spray for ages 2–49. 
    Key Information About Flu Shots: 
    • Availability: Shots are widely available at pharmacies (e.g., CVS, Walgreens), doctor's offices, and health clinics.
    • Types:
      For the 2024-2025 season, vaccines in the U.S. have transitioned to trivalent, protecting against three influenza strains.
    • Effectiveness: It takes about two weeks to build immunity. The CDC recommends getting vaccinated by the end of October, but vaccines still offer benefits later.
    • Side Effects: Common side effects are generally mild and include soreness at the injection site, headache, fatigue, or muscle pain.
    • Cost: The flu shot is covered at no cost by most insurance plans, including Medicare Part B. 
    Who Should Get the Shot: 
    • Everyone 6 months and older.
    • High-risk groups: Pregnant individuals, people over 65, and those with chronic health conditions (e.g., asthma, diabetes) should prioritize getting vaccinated. 
    Common Locations: 
    • CVS MinuteClinic
    • Walgreens
    • Safeway, Costco, Kroger, and more
    • Local health departments

    Side Effects. What are the side effects of the influenza vaccine?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Influenza vaccine side effects are generally mild, temporary, and indicate the body is building immunity. Common reactions include soreness, swelling, or redness at the injection site, low-grade fever, muscle aches, fatigue, and headache. These usually begin shortly after vaccination and resolve on their own within 1-2 days. 
    Common Side Effects
    • Injection Site Reactions: Pain, redness, swelling, or tenderness where the shot was given. 
    • Systemic Symptoms: Low-grade fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle aches, and headache. 
    • Other Potential Effects: Runny nose, sneezing, cough, sore throat, or loss of appetite (more common in children). 
    • Fainting: As with other injections, dizziness or fainting can occur. 
    Rare and Serious Side Effects
    • Allergic Reactions:
      Immediate, severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) are rare but possible, including hives, swelling of the face or throat, and difficulty breathing. 
    • Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS):
      A severe neurological condition that can occur very rarely following vaccination. 
    • Febrile Seizures:
      Very rarely associated with influenza vaccines in young children, often when given with other specific vaccines. 
    Important Considerations
    • Management: Most side effects are manageable and go away quickly, but a healthcare provider should be contacted if symptoms persist. 
    • Egg Allergies: Most flu vaccines are safe for people with egg allergies. 
    • Severe Reactions: Seek immediate medical attention for signs of a severe allergic reaction. 
    Side effects are a normal part of the body building immunity.

      Types. What are the different types of influenza vaccines?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Influenza vaccines include inactivated (flu shot), recombinant (egg-free), and live-attenuated (nasal spray) types, mostly designed as quadrivalent (four-strain) to cover influenza A and B. Options include standard dose, high-dose for seniors (65+), and adjuvanted versions for enhanced immune response, generally recommended for everyone six months and older. 
      Different Types of Influenza Vaccines
      • Inactivated Influenza Vaccines (IIV):
        The most common "flu shot," containing killed viruses. These are approved for people 6 months and older, including pregnant individuals. 
      • Recombinant Influenza Vaccine (RIV4):
        An egg-free vaccine created using genetic engineering, approved for adults 18 and older. 
      • Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine (LAIV4):
        A nasal spray vaccine containing weakened live viruses. It is approved for healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2 through 49 years. 
      • Cell-Based Flu Vaccine (ccIIV4):
        An inactivated vaccine produced in mammalian cells rather than eggs, offering an alternative for those with egg allergies. 
      • High-Dose Vaccine (HD-IIV4):
        Contains four times the antigen of a standard dose, designed for better protection in people 65 years and older. 
      • Adjuvanted Vaccine (aIIV4):
        Contains an ingredient (adjuvant) to create a stronger immune response, recommended for adults 65 and older. 
      Vaccine Formulations 
      • Quadrivalent:
        Protects against four strains (two A, two B). This is the standard formulation currently.
      • Trivalent:
        Protects against three strains (two A, one B). Use of trivalent vaccines is becoming less common.
      Most flu vaccines are egg-based, but cell-based and recombinant vaccines are completely egg-free. It is recommended to get vaccinated in early fall before the virus spreads.

        Timing. When should the influenza vaccine be administered?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        The influenza vaccine should ideally be administered in September or October before the virus begins spreading, with a goal of being vaccinated by the end of October. While early fall is best for most, vaccination can continue throughout the season, even into January or later. 
        Key Timing Recommendations:
        • Best Time: September and October. 
        • Why September/October: It takes about two weeks after vaccination for antibodies to develop. 
        • Avoid Early Vaccination: For most, July and August are too early, particularly for older adults, as protection may wane later in the season. 
        • Exceptions for Early Vaccination (July/August): Children needing two doses (who should start as soon as it's available) and people in their third trimester of pregnancy can get vaccinated earlier to protect their infants. 
        Important Considerations:
        • Target Group: Everyone aged 6 months and older should get a flu shot annually. 
        • Older Adults (65+): High-dose or adjuvanted vaccines are preferred, ideally in September/October. 
        • Vaccine Co-administration: Flu vaccines can be administered at the same time as COVID-19 vaccines.

          Benefits. What are the benefits of the influenza vaccine?
          Feedback
          INFLUENZA VACCINE (in floo EN zuh vak SEEN) reduces the risk of the influenza (flu). It does not treat influenza. It is still possible to get influenza after receiving this vaccine, but the symptoms may be less severe or not last as long. It works by helping your immune system learn how to fight off a future infection.
